title: Alma Redemptoris Mater
hook: the Marian antiphon of Advent and Christmas

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mother of the Church: behold thy mother, from the cross to the upper room. Your line was mother of the church. Who were you handed? Day one thousand three hundred thirty-five.

When the Church's night prayer is finished, there's one more thing before the silence: a short song to Mary, called an antiphon. Which one depends on the time of year, the way a coat does. In Advent, the dark weeks of waiting before Christmas, and on through the Christmas season, it's this one. It opens with three Latin words that climb slowly, like steps: Alma Redemptoris Mater. Loving mother of the Redeemer. Tradition credits it to a monk, Hermann of Reichenau. Over the next few days, the night song will change with the seasons, and we'll follow it around the year. Today's word is where it starts.
screen: `NIGHT PRAYER ENDS WITH A SONG TO MARY.` → `IT CHANGES WITH THE SEASON.` → `ADVENT AND CHRISTMAS: THIS ONE.`

segments.voice: Walk through it a phrase at a time. First, two pictures. The antiphon calls Mary the open gate of heaven, and stella maris, star of the sea. On a dark sea, sailors could steer by a star that stayed put while everything else moved. Advent is a season of waiting for light, and the song gives the people waiting a fixed point to steer by. Then the request, and it is honest. In Latin: succurre cadenti, surgere qui curat, populo. Help the people who are falling, who are trying to get up. Not a people who have it together. A people in the middle of falling, still trying to rise. Then the wonder. The song says that, while nature marveled, natura mirante, she gave birth to her own holy Creator. Sit with that for a second: a mother holding the one who made her. Nature doesn't explain it; nature marvels. That's Christmas, said in a single breath. And last, the song goes back to the beginning of the story. It remembers her taking that Ave from Gabriel's mouth, the angel's greeting in Luke's Gospel, which the Douay-Rheims gives as "Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with thee." Then it ends where a long day often ends, asking for mercy: peccatorum miserere, have mercy on sinners. Gate, star, falling and rising, wonder, mercy. A whole season, folded small enough to sing before bed.
screen: `GATE OF HEAVEN, STAR OF THE SEA.` · `HELP THE ONES FALLING, TRYING TO RISE.` · `NATURE MARVELS.` · `FROM GABRIEL'S MOUTH, AN AVE.` · then, large: `HAIL, FULL OF GRACE, THE LORD IS WITH THEE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: listen to it sung. If you can, find a recording of the Alma Redemptoris Mater in chant, and let it play. You don't need the Latin. Let your attention ride on the melody, the way a small boat rides a long wave. When you hear stella maris, let that be your star for a moment, the fixed point. If you can't play it now, say a few of its phrases slowly, one per breath: loving mother of the Redeemer. Gate of heaven. Star of the sea. Help the ones who fall and try to rise. If you pray, let it be your prayer. If you don't, let it simply be music in the dark. The bell holds the time.
Alma Redemptoris Mater. Loving mother of the Redeemer: the night song of Advent and Christmas, with its gate, its star, and its people falling and trying to rise. Today's word.
Your line: star of the sea. Today, name one fixed thing you steer by when the day gets choppy, and look to it once on purpose. Day one thousand three hundred thirty-five.

howItsDone: Catholics who pray the Liturgy of the Hours close Night Prayer with an antiphon to Mary; in Advent and the Christmas season it is traditionally the Alma Redemptoris Mater, often sung in Latin chant in monasteries and some parishes.
